title: Predicting Success: Dialing Long-Term Flourishing Back into Things We Might Affect This Year
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that if the real aim of schooling is the long-term flourishing of students, teachers need immediate signals that predict it, because they cannot wait twenty years for feedback. He makes the point with a thought experiment he has run with over a thousand educators: picture the student most likely to succeed and say why. Fewer than one percent name a cognitive skill; nearly everyone names noncognitive traits such as kindness, resilience, curiosity or self-direction. The move is from that gut-level consensus to a practical conclusion: if experts believe these factors determine success, they should be taught toward inside academic work. He ends by framing two follow-up questions, how to organize the long and idiosyncratic list and which factors are actually growable, and points to the Consortium Framework as the best answer.
points: Because long-term flourishing gives no quick feedback, teachers need nearer-term outcomes that reliably predict it, and the piece frames that search as the foundation of useful professional practice.
The thought experiment shows educators overwhelmingly explain future success with noncognitive traits rather than reading or math skill.
The raw list of traits is too long and idiosyncratic to act on, so it must be organized and sorted by which are growable and which matter most.
The author positions the Consortium Framework as the tool that can turn the intuition into a teachable structure.
quotes: If our ultimate goal is less than the long-term flourishing of kids, student motivation doesn’t matter much. English teachers want kids to become lifelong readers because we want them to flourish; science teachers aim at teaching a methodical way of thinking and viewing the world because such thinking is instrumental to a flourishing life; physical education exists because an unfit body makes it more difficult to flourish. And so on.

But here’s a big problem with long-term flourishing: I can’t very well get immediate feedback on whether or not the lessons I taught today will end up promoting the long-term flourishing of my students in twenty years. Useful feedback, it turns out, is kind of important.

At this point in my career, I’ve asked over a thousand educators to conduct this thought experiment, and the results are fascinating. Guess what percent of folks answer my question with a cognitive skill — something like “good reader,” “great at math,” “scientifically brilliant,” or “smart”? Less than one percent.
Which of them are growable? Which of them matter most? For my money, the Consortium Framework gives the clearest answers to these questions.

Our ability to collect and use it determines how much skill we’ll develop as teachers; it affects how motivated we’ll feel to keep doing the work each day. In other words, if we’re to productively work toward the long-term flourishing of our kids, we need to determine what types of outcomes in our immediate work are most able to predict whether our kids will flourish in the long-term.
